lessons.title: Big Countries
lessons.prompt: Return countries with area ≥ 3,000,000 OR population ≥ 25,000,000. Sort by name.
lessons.code: SELECT name FROM countries WHERE area >= 3000000 OR population >= 25000000 ORDER BY name;
lessons.postgres: SELECT name FROM countries WHERE area >= 3000000 OR population >= 25000000 ORDER BY name;
steps: FROM starts with every country.
WHERE retains a row satisfying either condition.
SELECT projects name; ORDER BY makes output deterministic.
lessons.trap: OR and AND express different contracts.

lessons.title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
lessons.prompt: Return IDs whose low_fats and recyclable flags are both Y; sort IDs.
lessons.code: SELECT id FROM products WHERE low_fats = 'Y' AND recyclable = 'Y' ORDER BY id;
lessons.postgres: SELECT id FROM products WHERE low_fats = 'Y' AND recyclable = 'Y' ORDER BY id;
steps: Filter both columns with AND.
Project the ID and sort it.
lessons.trap: Use single quotes for text literals.

lessons.title: Customers Who Never Order
lessons.prompt: Return customers with no order of any status, sorted by ID.
lessons.code:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.id;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.id;
steps: LEFT JOIN preserves each customer, even with no matched order.
Unmatched order IDs are NULL.
Filter the missing match and sort customer IDs.
lessons.trap: A filter on a right-table column in WHERE can unintentionally turn a LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

stages.name: After LEFT JOIN · matched and unmatched customers

lessons.title: Employees Earning More Than Managers
lessons.prompt: Return employees whose salary exceeds their manager’s salary; sort IDs.
lessons.code:
SELECT e.id, e.name
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary
ORDER BY e.id;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT e.id, e.name
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary
ORDER BY e.id;
steps: Use two aliases for the same table: employee and manager.
Join on the manager’s ID, not department.
Compare salaries; NULL salary comparisons do not evaluate True.
lessons.trap: A self-join represents two different roles, not duplicate output by itself.

stages.name: After self-join · the two salary roles

lessons.title: Duplicate Emails
lessons.prompt: Return each non-NULL email occurring more than once, sorted alphabetically.
lessons.code:
SELECT email
FROM contacts
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY email;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT email
FROM contacts
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY email;
steps: Exclude NULL emails before grouping.
Group identical emails and count rows.
HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
lessons.trap: WHERE filters input rows; HAVING filters aggregated groups.

lessons.title: Second Highest Salary
lessons.prompt: Return one row with the second-highest distinct non-NULL salary, or NULL if absent.
steps: The subquery obtains the highest salary.
Keep only salaries strictly below it, excluding all ties for first.
MAX on those remaining values is second highest; an empty aggregate yields NULL.
lessons.trap: Second employee is different from second distinct salary.

stages.name: After removing the highest distinct salary

lessons.title: Nth Highest Distinct Salary
lessons.prompt: For n=3, return the third-highest distinct salary, or NULL if absent.
steps: Filter NULL salaries before ranking.
DENSE_RANK assigns one consecutive rank per distinct salary.
Filter rank 3 in an outer query and use MAX to return exactly one row.
lessons.trap: Filter window results in an outer query or CTE, not the same SELECT’s WHERE.

lessons.title: Department Highest Salary
lessons.prompt: Return every employee tied for highest salary in each department. Sort department and employee IDs.
lessons.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS position
  FROM employees e WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT d.name AS department, r.name AS employee, r.salary
FROM ranked r JOIN departments d ON d.id = r.department_id
WHERE position = 1
ORDER BY d.id, r.id;
lessons.postgres:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS position
  FROM employees e WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT d.name AS department, r.name AS employee, r.salary
FROM ranked r JOIN departments d ON d.id = r.department_id
WHERE position = 1
ORDER BY d.id, r.id;
steps: PARTITION BY restarts ranking for each department.
Ranking excludes unknown salaries.
Join department labels and retain every rank-one row.
lessons.trap: ROW_NUMBER would arbitrarily keep one tie rather than all top earners.

stages.name: After department partitioning and dense ranking

lessons.title: Department Top Three Salaries
lessons.prompt: Return employees in each department’s top three distinct salary levels; keep ties.
lessons.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS position
  FROM employees e WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT department_id, name, salary
FROM ranked WHERE position <= 3
ORDER BY department_id, salary DESC, id;
lessons.postgres:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS position
  FROM employees e WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT department_id, name, salary
FROM ranked WHERE position <= 3
ORDER BY department_id, salary DESC, id;
steps: Rank distinct salaries independently per department.
Keep ranks 1–3, possibly yielding more than three employees.
Add a deterministic tie-breaker in the final ORDER BY.
lessons.trap: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK have different tie and gap semantics.

stages.name: All ranks before the top-three filter

lessons.title: Rank Scores
lessons.prompt: Return students and their dense rank by score, highest first; break output ties by ID.
steps: Use score alone in the window ordering so equal scores tie.
The outer ORDER BY includes ID for repeatable presentation.
lessons.trap: Adding ID to DENSE_RANK’s ORDER BY would destroy the score ties.

stages.name: Compare tie semantics · same input, three different rankings

lessons.title: Consecutive Numbers
lessons.prompt: Return numbers occurring in at least three consecutive log rows ordered by ID; return each once.
lessons.code:
WITH history AS (
  SELECT num, LAG(num,1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS previous,
         LAG(num,2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS two_back
  FROM logs
)
SELECT DISTINCT num FROM history
WHERE num = previous AND num = two_back ORDER BY num;
lessons.postgres:
WITH history AS (
  SELECT num, LAG(num,1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS previous,
         LAG(num,2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS two_back
  FROM logs
)
SELECT DISTINCT num FROM history
WHERE num = previous AND num = two_back ORDER BY num;
steps: LAG retrieves values one and two rows before the current row.
A current value matching both proves a run of three.
DISTINCT prevents a longer run from appearing repeatedly.
lessons.trap: This contract means consecutive rows in ID order, not necessarily consecutive numeric IDs.

stages.name: Window state · every current and prior value

lessons.title: Rising Temperature
lessons.prompt: Return weather IDs warmer than the previous calendar day; sort IDs.
lessons.code:
SELECT today.id
FROM weather today
JOIN weather yesterday ON today.record_date = date(yesterday.record_date, '+1 day')
WHERE today.temperature > yesterday.temperature
ORDER BY today.id;
steps: Self-join weather on a calendar-day relation.
Compare temperatures after joining the correct day.
lessons.trap: LAG alone compares the previous available row, which may not be the previous calendar day.

lessons.title: Managers With Five Direct Reports
lessons.prompt: Return manager IDs and names with at least five direct reports; sort IDs.
steps: Join employees to their direct managers.
Group the joined rows by manager.
HAVING checks the direct-report count.
lessons.trap: Descendants below direct reports are not counted by this join.

lessons.title: Classes With At Least Five Students
lessons.prompt: Return classes with at least five distinct students; sort course names.
lessons.code:
SELECT course FROM enrollment
GROUP BY course HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT student) >= 5 ORDER BY course;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT course FROM enrollment
GROUP BY course HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT student) >= 5 ORDER BY course;
steps: Group enrollments by course.
Count distinct student identifiers so duplicate enrollment records would not inflate the answer.
lessons.trap: COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT student) differ when duplicate records exist.

lessons.title: Confirmation Rate
lessons.prompt: For every signup, return confirmed attempts divided by all attempts, rounded to two decimals; no attempts means 0.
lessons.code:
SELECT s.user_id,
       ROUND(COALESCE(1.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
                      / NULLIF(COUNT(c.action),0), 0), 2) AS rate
FROM signups s LEFT JOIN confirmations c ON c.user_id = s.user_id
GROUP BY s.user_id ORDER BY s.user_id;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT s.user_id,
       ROUND(COALESCE(1.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
                      / NULLIF(COUNT(c.action),0), 0), 2) AS rate
FROM signups s LEFT JOIN confirmations c ON c.user_id = s.user_id
GROUP BY s.user_id ORDER BY s.user_id;
steps: LEFT JOIN includes users with no attempts.
CASE counts confirmed attempts; COUNT(c.action) ignores the NULL placeholder for no match.
Use 1.0 to force noninteger division, NULLIF for a zero denominator, then COALESCE.
lessons.trap: COUNT(*) would count the unmatched placeholder row. PostgreSQL may need a numeric cast when adapting floating expressions for ROUND.

stages.name: After LEFT JOIN · note the NULL row for signup 3

lessons.title: Paid Revenue by Customer
lessons.prompt: Include every customer. Sum only paid order amounts; customers without paid orders receive zero.
lessons.code:
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount),0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount),0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY c.id;
steps: Put the paid-status restriction inside ON to preserve unmatched customers.
Group each customer’s paid matches.
SUM over no matches is NULL; COALESCE converts it to zero.
lessons.trap: WHERE o.status = paid would remove zero-revenue customers.

stages.name: After paid-only LEFT JOIN · zero-revenue customers remain

lessons.title: Running Revenue
lessons.prompt: Aggregate paid revenue by date, then show its cumulative total in chronological order.
lessons.code:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY order_date
)
SELECT order_date, revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM daily ORDER BY order_date;
lessons.postgres:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY order_date
)
SELECT order_date, revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM daily ORDER BY order_date;
steps: First collapse multiple orders on one date into one daily row.
Then sum the daily values over an explicit growing ROWS frame.
lessons.trap: Aggregates collapse rows; window aggregates retain each row. Use an explicit frame when duplicates matter.

stages.name: Daily CTE before applying the cumulative window

lessons.title: Rolling Two-Row Average
lessons.prompt: For each paid-revenue date, show the average of that row and the preceding revenue row, rounded to two decimals.
lessons.code:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY order_date
)
SELECT order_date,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) AS moving_average
FROM daily ORDER BY order_date;
lessons.postgres:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY order_date
)
SELECT order_date,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) AS moving_average
FROM daily ORDER BY order_date;
steps: Group daily revenue before applying the window.
The first row has only itself in its frame.
The next row averages two revenue rows.
lessons.trap: Two rows is not necessarily two calendar days if dates are missing.

stages.name: Daily rows before evaluating each two-row frame

lessons.title: First Login per Player
lessons.prompt: Return each player’s first login date, sorted by player ID.
lessons.code:
SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_login
FROM activity GROUP BY player_id ORDER BY player_id;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_login
FROM activity GROUP BY player_id ORDER BY player_id;
steps: Group by player ID and take the earliest date.
lessons.trap: The sample stores dates in ISO YYYY-MM-DD text; its lexical ordering matches calendar ordering.

lessons.title: Next-Day Retention
lessons.prompt: Return the fraction of players who log in on the day immediately after their first login, rounded to two decimals.
steps: Create one first-login row per player.
EXISTS tests next-calendar-day activity without multiplying the player row.
Average the one/zero indicators.
lessons.trap: Joining all later activity can double count players. EXISTS preserves one vote per player.

lessons.title: Product Sales Totals
lessons.prompt: Return total quantity and revenue by product ID, sorted by product ID.
lessons.code:
SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units, SUM(revenue) AS revenue
FROM sales GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY product_id;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units, SUM(revenue) AS revenue
FROM sales GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY product_id;
steps: Group repeated product sales into one row.
Aggregate quantity and revenue independently.
lessons.trap: Do not SUM unit price when the contract asks for revenue.

lessons.title: Employees Above Department Average
lessons.prompt: Return non-NULL-salary employees whose salary is above their department’s average, sorted by ID.
steps: Calculate one average per department; AVG ignores NULL salaries.
Join each employee to their department statistic.
Keep only salaries strictly above it.
lessons.trap: A correlated subquery or window AVG can express the same logic.

stages.name: One average per department · NULL salaries excluded by AVG

lessons.title: Find Redundant Email Records
lessons.prompt: For non-NULL duplicate emails, keep the lowest ID and return the redundant IDs.
steps: Exclude NULL emails because this contract treats missing emails independently.
ROW_NUMBER picks an unambiguous first record using ID.
Return later records without deleting anything.
lessons.trap: Ranking is a read-only preview here. Real deletion would require a carefully scoped transaction.

stages.name: Every numbered non-NULL email record before filtering

lessons.title: UNION Versus UNION ALL
lessons.prompt: Combine names from employees ID ≤ 2 and customers ID ≤ 3. Return each distinct name once, alphabetically.
lessons.code:
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE id <= 2
UNION
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id <= 3
ORDER BY name;
lessons.postgres:
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE id <= 2
UNION
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id <= 3
ORDER BY name;
steps: Each SELECT projects a compatible name column.
UNION removes duplicate complete result rows.
The final ORDER BY applies to the combined result.
lessons.trap: UNION ALL preserves duplicates and often avoids deduplication work.

lessons.title: Consecutive Login Streaks
lessons.prompt: Return runs of at least two consecutive calendar login days per player. Deduplicate same-day logins first.
lessons.postgres:
WITH days AS (SELECT DISTINCT player_id,event_date::date AS event_date FROM activity),
numbered AS (
 SELECT player_id,event_date,
 event_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_date))::integer AS island
 FROM days
)
SELECT player_id,MIN(event_date) AS start_day,MAX(event_date) AS end_day,COUNT(*) AS length
FROM numbered GROUP BY player_id,island HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY player_id,start_day;
steps: Remove repeated login dates before assigning row numbers.
For consecutive days, calendar ordinal minus row number stays constant.
Group that island key and retain qualifying runs.
lessons.trap: Day ordinals are SQLite julianday here. PostgreSQL uses date arithmetic; the two versions are shown explicitly.

foundations: Logical query order
FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window calculations → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. This is a reasoning model, not the physical execution plan.
NULL and three-valued logic
= NULL is not a NULL check. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL. WHERE retains only True; False and Unknown are rejected. COUNT(column) ignores NULL; COUNT(*) counts rows.
Anti-joins
NOT EXISTS avoids the NULL trap in NOT IN. If a NOT IN subquery returns NULL, otherwise-unmatched comparisons can become Unknown.
Join multiplicity
One-to-many joins multiply rows. Aggregate each many-side first when joining multiple detail tables, or you can multiply sums. DISTINCT is not a universal fix.
LEFT JOIN filters
A right-side filter in WHERE can discard unmatched rows. Put matching restrictions in ON when you must preserve every left-side row.
Grouping
Every selected nonaggregate expression must be grouped or supported by the engine’s functional-dependency rules. Write explicit GROUP BY columns for portable clarity.
Ranking
ROW_NUMBER numbers every row; include a deterministic tie-breaker. RANK leaves gaps after ties. DENSE_RANK has no gaps between distinct levels.
Window frames
ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE groups peer values under ordering. Explicit ROWS frames avoid surprising cumulative totals on tied sort keys.
Integer division and zero
Cast or multiply by 1.0 before dividing integer counts. Use NULLIF(denominator,0), then decide whether NULL or zero is the intended result.
Date dialects
The verified sample queries use SQLite with ISO date text. PostgreSQL references use casts, date + integer or intervals. MySQL date functions differ; confirm the actual assessment dialect.
CTEs and subqueries
CTEs name intermediate relations and improve readability. Do not assume they always materialise or always improve performance; inspect the plan.
Indexes and EXPLAIN
Indexes can help filters/joins/order, but add write and storage cost. Composite-key order matters. Use EXPLAIN to inspect access strategy; PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query.
Transactions and constraints
BEGIN/COMMIT make a unit of work atomic; ROLLBACK undoes it. UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK express invariants. Isolation level determines allowed concurrent anomalies.
Safe parameterisation
Pass values as bound parameters via your database driver. Do not interpolate untrusted input into SQL. Parameters represent values, not arbitrary identifiers.
